[34]                        The plain words of this provision are unambiguous. Section 5(1)(a) provides that no claim shall be brought after two years from the day on which the claim is “discovered”. Section 5(2) further specifies that a claim is discovered on the day that a claimant knew or ought reasonably to have known the facts that are material, namely the occurrence of an injury, loss or damage that was caused or contributed to by an act or omission of the defendant. As evidenced by the words of the provision, there is no clear legislative language ousting or limiting the common law rule; in fact, quite the opposite. The event triggering the limitation period in s. 5(1)(a) is linked to the state of the plaintiff’s knowledge in the same manner as the common law rule.

Held: The appeals should be allowed and the motions judge’s judgment restored.

                    The standard to be applied in determining whether a plaintiff has the requisite degree of knowledge to discover a claim under s. 5(2) of the LAA, thereby triggering the two‑year limitation period in s. 5(1)(a), is whether the plaintiff has knowledge, actual or constructive, of the material facts upon which a plausible inference of liability on the defendant’s part can be drawn. Applying this standard in the present case, the province discovered its claim against the auditor on February 4, 2011. By then, it knew or ought to have known that a loss occurred and that the loss was caused in whole or in part by conduct which the auditor had been retained to detect. This was sufficient to draw a plausible inference that the auditor had been negligent. Since the province did not bring its claim until June 23, 2014, more than two years later, its claim is therefore statute‑barred.

facts.text: The claimant experienced incapacitation at the time the right to bring an action arose.
facts.why_it_matters: Under section 15 of the Limitations Act, if a person is under a disability when the right to bring an action arises, the running of the limitation period is postponed for as long as the disability continues. This could potentially extend the time to bring the claim.
facts.if_changed: If the claimant was not under a disability at the time the right to bring an action arose, the limitation period would begin to run immediately, and the claim could be time-barred unless another exception applies.

facts.text: The claimant discovered material evidence decades after the initial incident.
facts.why_it_matters: Under section 14(1) of the Limitations Act, the limitation period does not begin to run until the claimant knows or ought to know that they have a cause of action. If the claimant only discovered material evidence later, this could delay the start of the limitation period.
facts.if_changed: If the claimant had discovered the material evidence earlier, the limitation period would have started to run at that earlier date, potentially barring the claim if it was not brought within the applicable time frame.

facts.text: The claimant was aware of the material facts underlying the claim at the time of the incident.
facts.why_it_matters: If the claimant was aware of the material facts at the time of the incident, the limitation period would have started to run from that date, and the discovery of later evidence may not be sufficient to extend the limitation period.
facts.if_changed: If the claimant was not aware of the material facts at the time of the incident, the limitation period could be delayed under the discoverability principle, potentially extending the time to bring the claim.

facts.text: The claimant is now no longer under a disability.
facts.why_it_matters: If the claimant has since ceased to be under a disability, the limitation period would resume running from the date the disability ended. The claim must be brought within the remaining time.
facts.if_changed: If the claimant is still under a disability, the limitation period would continue to be postponed, potentially allowing more time to bring the claim.

facts.text: The claimant has not yet brought the action within the limitation period.
facts.why_it_matters: If the claimant has not brought the action within the limitation period, the claim may be time-barred unless an exception applies, such as disability or discovery of material evidence.
facts.if_changed: If the claimant had brought the action within the limitation period, the claim would not be time-barred, and the court would proceed to assess the merits of the case.

facts.text: The claim is for personal injury.
facts.why_it_matters: Personal injury claims are subject to specific rules under the Limitations Act, including the discoverability principle and the possibility of tolling due to disability.
facts.if_changed: If the claim were for a different type of damage, such as property damage, the rules for limitation periods might differ, potentially affecting the analysis.

facts.text: The claimant has the burden of proving that the limitation period was postponed or suspended.
facts.why_it_matters: Under section 14(2) and section 15(2) of the Limitations Act, the claimant must prove that the limitation period was postponed or suspended, such as due to disability or discovery of material evidence.
facts.if_changed: If the claimant cannot prove that the limitation period was postponed or suspended, the claim may be time-barred, and the court may dismiss it on that basis.

facts.text: The claim was not brought within 10 years of the act or omission.
facts.why_it_matters: Under section 14(3) of the Limitations Act, an action included in subsection (1) shall not be taken by a person after the expiration of 10 years from the later of the date of the act or omission or the termination of a continuing course of conduct.
facts.if_changed: If the claim was brought within 10 years of the act or omission, it may still be valid, even if the limitation period was extended due to disability or discovery of evidence.
